mundane

/muhn-DAYN/ - the stress falls on DAYN · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Mundane means ordinary and commonplace — the plain, unexciting business of everyday life.

She loved how the astronauts' checklists made orbit sound mundane: wipe the filter, log the reading, stow the trash.

Example

The internship posting promised rocket science, but Dana's August was mundane: she relabeled sample jars, refilled the printer tray, and alphabetized a cabinet of old launch permits while the engineers worked behind glass.

Nothing in her week is difficult or strange — it is the ordinary, unexciting paperwork any office generates, and that flat everydayness is exactly what mundane names. The word usually carries a small sigh: the speaker expected, or at least hoped for, something more.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

ordinary: Ordinary means unremarkable — a neutral report that nothing here stands out. Mundane adds a faint shrug of dullness: the flatness of chores, errands, and paperwork, felt as flatness.

routine: Routine means done as a regular procedure, by habit or schedule. Mundane is about how uninteresting a thing feels, not how regularly it happens — a routine task can still thrill, and a mundane one can be a one-off.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

extraordinary: far beyond the ordinary

exotic: strikingly unfamiliar, from somewhere else entirely

Where it sits · how heavily the dullness weighs

everyday → mundane → humdrum

everyday vs. mundane: Everyday is milder than mundane: everyday tasks are simply the normal round, stated without complaint, while calling them mundane adds the first sigh of dullness.

humdrum vs. mundane: Humdrum goes further than mundane: a mundane job is merely unexciting, while a humdrum one drones — the sameness has thickened into wearying monotony.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — mund-: the world (Latin mundus)

Suffix — -ane: of, belonging to (Latin -anus)

Put it together: Mund- (Latin mundus, 'the world') + -ane (of, belonging to) = of the world. Medieval writers split existence into heaven's business and the world's, and mundane took the lower half — rent, roads, laundry. Centuries of that duty wore it down from 'worldly' to 'ordinary and unexciting.' The root built almost nothing else in everyday English, so meet it in a museum piece below.

Use the root in a museum piece: mappa mundi: The cathedral's medieval mappa mundi crowds oceans, kingdoms, and sea monsters onto a single sheet of calf-skin.

Strength Check

Word Choice

conversational / faintly dismissive

Mundane files a small complaint: this is ordinary, and the speaker noticed. Quotidian, taught in this unit, covers the same daily ground with scholarly affection rather than a sigh. And careful writers still use the root's old contrast — mundane concerns are worldly ones, rent and receipts and logistics, set against matters of the spirit.
